title: Operation Summer '95: The Fall of Grahovo and Glamoč
sources: ICTY Gotovina et al. Trial Judgment (IT-06-90-T)
content:
In the last week of July 1995, Croatian Army and HVO forces launched Operation Summer '95 against VRS positions in the Livanjsko Polje region of western Bosnia. The offensive targeted two strategically vital towns — Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoč — whose capture would sever the main road linking Knin, capital of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to Banja Luka and the broader Bosnian Serb hinterland. Within five days, both towns had fallen and approximately 1,600 square kilometers of territory had changed hands.

The operation was spearheaded by some of Croatia's most capable formations. The HV 4th Guards Brigade and 7th Guards Brigade, veterans of Operation Flash in May 1995, provided the assault force. These units had been retrained and reequipped over the preceding years and represented a qualitative leap from the improvised Croatian forces of 1991. HVO units from western Herzegovina participated in supporting roles, reflecting the close coordination between Zagreb and the Bosnian Croat military establishment that had been formalized through the Washington Agreement's Federation framework in 1994.

The VRS defenders in the Grahovo-Glamoč sector were outmatched. The Bosnian Serb army, by mid-1995, was stretched across an enormous front line while simultaneously conducting operations against the eastern enclaves. The 2nd Krajina Corps, responsible for this sector, lacked the reserves to mount an effective defense against a concentrated Croatian assault. Grahovo fell on 28 July. Glamoč followed on 29 July. The speed of the collapse alarmed the VRS General Staff, but there was little that could be done — reinforcements were unavailable and the strategic initiative had shifted decisively.

The significance of the operation extended far beyond the territory seized. By cutting the Knin-Banja Luka road, Croatian forces severed the last practical supply and communication route between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska. The RSK, already weakened by the loss of Western Slavonia in Operation Flash, was now strategically isolated. Its military position had become untenable. The ICTY proceedings in Gotovina et al. (IT-06-90-T) examined the broader Croatian military campaign of 1995, including the operational planning that connected Summer '95 to the far larger Operation Storm that followed days later.

The fall of Grahovo and Glamoč also triggered a political crisis within the Republika Srpska leadership. President Radovan Karadžić blamed General Ratko Mladić for the losses and attempted to remove him from command — a confrontation that would paralyze the Bosnian Serb command structure at its most vulnerable moment. The VRS officer corps rallied behind Mladić, and Karadžić was ultimately forced to relent, but the episode exposed deep fractures between the political and military leaderships of the Serb entity.

For the Federation, the operation demonstrated that the military balance in Bosnia had shifted irreversibly. The VRS could no longer defend its extended territorial holdings against coordinated, well-equipped offensives. The stage was set for the cascade of operations — Storm, Mistral 2, Sana — that would compress Republika Srpska to roughly half of Bosnia's territory and create the military conditions for the Dayton peace settlement.
